answer.label: Not Vince Lombardi — the trail leads to Fielding H. Yost
answer.authorDates: 1871–1946 · University of Michigan football coach & athletic director
answer.sourceLine: Quote Investigator names Michigan coach Fielding H. Yost as the leading candidate for the saying, documenting it in his 1929–30 Wingate Memorial Lecture and a February 1930 address — decades before anyone attached it to Lombardi. Yost’s own phrasing was looser; the tight modern wording is a later compression by unknown hands.
answer.confidenceText: Documented with Yost in 1930; first pinned on Lombardi in 1996, 26 years after his death.

source.excerpt: The will and the wish to win, but there isn’t a chance for either one of them to be gratified or to have any value unless there has been a will to prepare to win.
trail: 1929–30 — Fielding H. Yost tells a Wingate Memorial Lecture audience that the will and wish to win are worthless “unless there has been a will to prepare to win,” per Quote Investigator ↗.

13 February 1930 — Yost repeats the thought in a Philadelphia address later printed in The Barnwell Addresses (1931): the will to win “is not of much worth unless you have the will to prepare” (QI citation ↗).
2002 — Bobby Knight publishes his own version in Knight: My Story, as sourced by Wikiquote ↗ — evidence of how widely coaches had adopted the maxim.
Today — the compressed one-liner circulates under Lombardi, Bryant, Knight and Paterno; the official Lombardi quote collection ↗ does not include it.
source.excerptNote: And from Yost’s February 1930 Barnwell address: “Preparation—that is the big thing. It is all right to talk about this ‘will to win,’ but I tell you it is not of much worth unless you have the will to prepare.” Both passages were located and dated by Quote Investigator; the compact modern wording matches neither exactly.
source.rightsNote: The exact popular wording has no identified author — it is a compressed paraphrase that appeared long after Yost, so no copyright status can honestly be asserted for it. Yost’s own documented 1930 lecture text, published in the United States in 1930, is itself out of copyright; the 1931 Barnwell Addresses printing is a separate, later publication.

author.name: Fielding H. Yost
author.kicker: The coach who actually said it
author.heading: Who was Fielding H. Yost?
author.bio: Fielding Harris Yost coached the University of Michigan Wolverines from 1901 to 1923 and again in 1925–26, compiling a 165–29–10 record there and six national titles, including the legendary “Point-a-Minute” teams of 1901–1905. He served as Michigan’s athletic director from 1921 to 1940 and was inducted into the College Football Hall of Fame in 1951. Preparation was his signature theme — the idea that wanting to win is worthless without the discipline to get ready for it recurs across his surviving lectures.

misattribution.heading: How it ended up on Lombardi’s name
misattribution.intro: This is a coaching maxim with a long documented life before Vince Lombardi’s name was attached to it. It circulates under at least four famous names — three of them coaches, plus a self-help author — in at least four different wordings.

items.why: Lombardi died in 1970. Quote Investigator ↗ finds the earliest attribution of the saying to Lombardi in The Odessa American of October 17, 1996 — twenty-six years after his death — in the form “Everyone has the will to win but very few have the will to prepare to win.” The line does not appear on the official Lombardi family quote page ↗.

The variant “It’s not the will to win that matters—everyone has that. It’s the will to prepare to win that matters” is widely posted under Bryant’s name, for instance at PassItOn ↗, with no primary source given.
That identical variant is filed on Goodreads ↗ under Jack Canfield’s The Success Principles — one saying, two authors, on two major quote sites.

Knight’s phrasing — “The key is not the will to win… everybody has that. It is the will to prepare to win that is important” — is sourced by Wikiquote ↗ to his 2002 book Knight: My Story, long after the idea was in circulation.

misattribution.truthLine: The documented trail leads to Fielding H. Yost, whom Quote Investigator ↗ calls the leading candidate for creator of the saying — though even Yost’s own wording was longer and looser than the slogan we quote today.

context.heading: Why this one stuck to Lombardi
lead: Yost never said it this crisply. What he said, in a 1929–30 coaching lecture, was that the will and the wish to win have no value “unless there has been a will to prepare to win” — and a few months later, on a Philadelphia stage, that it is fine to talk about the will to win, “but I tell you it is not of much worth unless you have the will to prepare.” The modern one-liner is those two thoughts filed down to a slogan.

Once filed down, it went looking for a bigger name. Coaches repeated it for decades in their own words, and by the 1990s it had drifted onto the marquee names of American sport — Lombardi, Bear Bryant, Bobby Knight, Joe Paterno. Lombardi is the classic destination for orphaned winning-and-discipline lines, and this one arrived there long after he was gone.
detailsBody: Bobby Knight’s version — “The key is not the will to win… everybody has that. It is the will to prepare to win that is important” — is genuinely his: it appears in his own 2002 memoir Knight: My Story. That makes him a documented user of the idea, not its originator.

Attribution drift on this saying is unusually messy. The same variant is credited on quote sites to Bear Bryant on one page and Jack Canfield on another. That kind of contradiction is a reliable signal that a line has slipped loose from its source.
